# Scalability & Extensibility

The solution is modular in structure and selectively parametrized in behaviour. Modularity concerns which responsibilities can be changed 
independently, whereas parametrization changes the behaviour of an existing component without changing its code. The backend separates database 
context loading, deterministic engines, targeted LLM steps, Advisor tools, prompts, session persistence, and observability. These boundaries are
functional rather than cosmetic. The modal-shift engine, for example, receives the feasibility judge as an optional callable and can therefore run with 
the LLM implementation, a test double, or its deterministic fallback without importing a model client. The same scoring primitive is reused by the
initial analysis, modal-shift ranking, and chat-driven re-optimization, so a scoring correction propagates through all three paths instead of being 
reimplemented per workflow.

Behaviour within those modules is parametrized at several levels. The three onboarding priorities become normalized cost, CO~2~, and time 
weights. The forecast horizon and output language are function inputs. What-if requests pass `keep`, `drop`, `prefer_plans`, and `exclude_plans` 
constraints into the same re-optimization engine. Operational settings such as the model endpoint, database-pool size, worker count, LLM concurrency, 
timeouts, and retries are environment variables rather than constants at their call sites. This makes the solution adaptable, but not fully configuration-driven. 
The Advisor's seven-tool registry is explicit. Adding a capability requires a new deterministic tool, registration in the Advisor, a prompt instruction, and tests. 
Likewise, a new provider whose tariff fits an existing category and pricing model can normally be added as a catalogue row and an OKF Markdown document, while a 
new mobility category, scoring dimension, or pricing model crosses coverage maps, reference factors, engines, prompts, and frontend presentation and therefore still 
requires code changes.

The current design contains several measures that support moderate growth. Per-user database queries are indexed, PostgreSQL connections are pooled, 
and the mostly static pricing catalogue is cached. A stored session snapshot acts as a read-through cache, so reopening the dashboard does not automatically 
repeat the analysis or its model calls. On a fresh analysis, the deterministic result is returned before the slower enrichment begins. Forecast reasoning and 
modal-shift feasibility then run concurrently on background workers. A process-wide LLM concurrency limit queues excess calls instead of overwhelming the 
shared university endpoint. These choices improve latency and protect the pilot under bursts, but the limit is a reliability control rather than additional 
throughput.

Larger production volumes would expose boundaries that are insignificant for the ten-persona prototype. `load_context` currently retrieves a user's complete 
leg-level history and aggregates it in Python. A longer history should be filtered and pre-aggregated in SQL or materialized views. Tariff retrieval scans the
Markdown tree and reads complete documents, which is appropriate for the present corpus but would need a persistent metadata or full-text index, document chunking, 
and selective context at much larger scale. Long conversations also accumulate messages and tool observations in the checkpointer, so production use would require 
retention rules, context windows, or conversation summaries. Finally, background enrichment, catalogue caches, and the LLM semaphore live inside one backend process. 
Horizontal scaling would therefore require a durable external job queue, centrally coordinated rate limits, and multiple stateless API instances behind a load balancer 
rather than merely increasing the local thread count. The free university-hosted LLM endpoint is suitable for the prototype but does not provide the capacity or service 
guarantees needed for production scale. A larger deployment would require either an agreed production quota, a commercial OpenAI-compatible provider, or a self-hosted 
model. Since model access is centralized in `agent/llm.py` and the model identifier and base URL are configurable, such a change would leave the deterministic engines 
and Advisor tools intact, but the replacement would still need to be re-evaluated for structured-output reliability, tool selection, latency, privacy, and cost.

Maintainability benefits from the same separation of concerns. `agent/llm.py` centralizes model access and retry policy, `session.py` owns snapshots, transcripts, 
and revisions, prompts have a local versioned fallback, and deterministic engines can be tested without a database or model endpoint. The explicit simulate--confirm--apply
boundary also isolates the only state-changing capability. Two limitations remain. Most internal contracts are nested dictionaries, so typed models would make schema changes 
across pipeline, tools, snapshots, and frontend safer. Some legacy names and compatibility structures also survive, including the unused root-level `analyst_agent.py` and an 
`optimizer_scenarios` database column whose payload has since changed. Removing those artefacts and replacing first-run SQL initialization with managed schema migrations 
would make the otherwise clear module boundaries easier to maintain as the system grows.
